name: Duke Energy Corporation

profile.description: Duke Energy is one of the largest regulated electric and natural gas utilities in the United States, serving approximately 8.4 million customers across six states through its Electric Utilities and Infrastructure (EU&I) and Gas Utilities and Infrastructure (GU&I) segments. The company generates, transmits, and distributes electricity from a diversified fuel mix including nuclear, natural gas, coal, hydroelectric, and renewables. Full-year 2025 revenue of $32.2B with adjusted EPS of $6.31 reflects the regulated utility model. Duke has secured 7.8 GW of data center service agreements with an additional 15.4 GW pipeline. Founded in 1904 and headquartered in Charlotte, North Carolina [1][3].

innovation.label: WEAK
innovation.analysis: Track Record (1/3): Duke Energy has made incremental progress on the clean energy transition — investing in grid modernization, expanding renewable generation, and retiring coal plants — but these are industry-mandated adaptations rather than distinctive innovations [3]. The $103B five-year capital plan is large in absolute terms but standard for major regulated utilities. No transformative business model pivots or new market entries in the last five years. AI Deployment (0/2): No evidence of AI-powered products or services deployed to customers. Duke operates a traditional regulated utility model without meaningful AI deployment in customer-facing or operational applications beyond standard grid management tools. Market Share (1/2): Duke is among the three largest regulated electric utilities in the U.S., serving 8.4 million customers across six states with a de facto geographic monopoly in its service territories [3]. However, in a regulated utility, market share is assigned by regulatory franchise rather than earned through competition, limiting the innovation signal. Product Pipeline (1/2): Duke has secured 7.8 GW of data center electric service agreements with a 15.4 GW late-stage pipeline expected to convert by H1 2027, representing $5-10B in potential capital plan additions [1][2]. Small modular reactor and offshore wind initiatives are in early stages. However, these are capacity additions within the existing regulated model, not new products. R&D Intensity (0/1): Regulated utilities generally invest minimally in R&D as a percentage of revenue, with capital directed toward infrastructure maintenance and expansion rather than research. Duke does not disclose a separate R&D line item [3].

inspiration.label: WEAK
inspiration.analysis: Mission Floor (1/4): Duke Energy's purpose revolves around powering the lives of customers and the vitality of communities. This is a generic utility mission statement — essentially interchangeable with any other regulated electric utility. It describes the business (delivering power) rather than articulating a distinctive vision of a better future [3]. Community & Charitable Impact (1/2): Duke Energy Foundation is a well-established corporate philanthropic entity in the Southeast, supporting education, workforce development, and environmental stewardship programs across its service territories. While specific program dollar amounts were not available in searches, Duke's community presence as a 122-year-old utility serving 8.4 million customers represents meaningful institutional investment in its communities [3]. Employee Retention & Tenure (0/2): Duke has 26,441 employees and operates as a regulated utility with union representation, which typically supports stable employment. However, no specific voluntary turnover, average tenure, or culture data was found to distinguish Duke from utility industry norms. Insider Buying (0/2): No evidence of meaningful net insider buying by CEO or senior executives was found in searches. A leadership transition from Lynn Good (CEO since 2013) to Harry Sideris (effective April 2024) was executed as a planned succession.

infrastructure.label: STRONG
infrastructure.analysis: Mechanically scored as a Dividend stock. Duke Energy's financial profile reflects the classic regulated utility model — lower returns offset by regulatory visibility and dividend reliability. D/E of 162.2% is elevated but typical for capital-intensive utilities (score 0.60) [4]. ROE of 9.9% is below the 15% target (score 0.66), constrained by the regulated return structure. Revenue growth of 1.1% YoY for the most recent quarter reflects the slow-growth nature of regulated utilities (score 0.70), while the estimated 5-year revenue CAGR of 5.0% includes some energy price fluctuations (score 0.67) [1][4]. Forward P/E of 16.9 is well below the 20 target (score 1.0), reflecting utility valuation norms. Profit margin of 16.0% approaches but falls short of the 20% target (score 0.80). The dividend profile is mixed but durable: payout ratio of 64.2% is above the 40% ideal but standard for utilities (score 0.60), 43 consecutive years paid (score 1.0, 2x weight), 20 consecutive years of growth (score 1.0), and 5-year dividend growth CAGR of 2.0% is well below the 6% target (score 0.33, 2x weight) [4]. Liquidity is excellent at $501.8M daily dollar volume.

ai_resilience.label: LOW RISK
ai_resilience.analysis: AI Risk Protection (9/9): Duke Energy's regulated electric and gas utility business is IMMUNE to AI disruption. AI cannot replace the physical generation, transmission, and distribution of electricity — power plants, transmission lines, substations, and distribution networks are irreplaceable physical infrastructure protected by regulatory franchises and multi-decade investment cycles [3]. No analyst has flagged AI as a substitution risk for regulated utilities. In fact, AI dramatically increases demand for Duke's core product: data centers require massive electricity consumption, and Duke has already secured 7.8 GW of data center service agreements with a 15.4 GW pipeline [1][2]. This positions Duke as a direct beneficiary of AI infrastructure buildout. The regulated utility model — where customer rates are set by public utility commissions based on invested capital plus allowed return — provides structural insulation from any technology disruption. AI Opportunity (1/1): Duke generates quantifiable revenue from AI-related infrastructure. The 7.8 GW of data center service agreements, with some including minimum-take provisions, represent billions in committed future electricity sales to AI infrastructure customers [1][2]. Management estimates these agreements could add $5-10B to the five-year capital plan. While Duke sells electricity rather than AI products, the company is directly monetizing AI's insatiable demand for power.

infinite_game.summary: Duke Energy plays a mixed infinite game. The company has powered communities for 122 years through multiple energy transformations — from coal to nuclear to natural gas to renewables — demonstrating genuine endurance and purpose. The $103B five-year capital plan and commitment to clean energy transition show long-term thinking. However, regulated utilities operate within a fundamentally constrained model where regulators set returns, limiting the scope for courageous leadership or existential flexibility. The company's cause is legitimate but generic, and the competitive dynamics of a regulated monopoly do not test the infinite game principles that Sinek values most.

just_cause.analysis: Just Cause (2/3): Duke Energy has powered the lives of its customers and communities for 122 years, enduring through the Great Depression, two World Wars, energy crises, deregulation debates, and now the clean energy transition [3]. The purpose of providing reliable, affordable energy has been consistently pursued through multiple leadership transitions and industry transformations — from coal to nuclear to gas to renewables. The cause is genuine and has been validated by over a century of execution. However, it falls short of a 3-point Just Cause because it is inherent to the regulated utility model rather than a distinctive competitive advantage — every utility serves this same purpose by regulatory mandate.

trusting_teams.analysis: Trusting Teams (1/2): Duke Energy's planned CEO succession from Lynn Good (2013-2024) to Harry Sideris was executed smoothly with multi-year preparation, signaling organizational maturity [3]. The company's 26,441 employees operate in a stable, unionized environment typical of regulated utilities, which generally provides job security and predictable career paths. However, no specific employee satisfaction, voluntary turnover, or cultural excellence data distinguishes Duke from utility industry norms.

worthy_rivals.analysis: Worthy Rivals (0/1): Regulated utilities do not have direct competitors in the traditional sense — Duke operates as a geographic monopoly in its service territories. The concept of a worthy rival that pushes self-improvement does not naturally apply to a regulated monopoly. Duke benchmarks against industry peers for operational efficiency, but there is no evidence of the kind of competitive learning mindset that Sinek describes [3].

existential_flexibility.analysis: Existential Flexibility (1/2): Duke Energy is navigating the clean energy transition — retiring coal plants, building renewable generation, investing in grid modernization, and positioning for nuclear expansion including small modular reactors [1][3]. The $103B five-year capital plan commits to transforming the generation fleet over decades. The pivot from coal to a diversified clean energy portfolio represents meaningful strategic evolution. However, this transition is being driven by regulation and market forces rather than voluntary cause-driven reinvention, and the underlying regulated utility business model remains fundamentally unchanged.

courage_to_lead.analysis: Courage to Lead (1/2): Duke Energy's $103B five-year capital plan, increased by $16B in the latest revision, represents a significant long-term investment commitment in grid modernization and clean energy [1][3]. Securing 7.8 GW of data center agreements demonstrates proactive positioning for AI-driven demand growth. Reaffirming 5-7% long-term EPS growth targets while investing $103B shows capital allocation discipline. However, these investments are partially mandated by regulators and funded through rate recovery, reducing the true risk to management. The courage to lead test is softer for regulated utilities where returns are guaranteed by the rate-setting process.

investment_thesis: Duke Energy at $121 with a $94.6B market cap is one of America's largest regulated utilities positioned as a direct beneficiary of AI-driven electricity demand growth. The company has secured 7.8 GW of data center service agreements with a 15.4 GW late-stage pipeline, representing potential $5-10B in capital plan additions — these agreements include minimum-take provisions that underpin revenue growth projections [1][2]. Adjusted EPS of $6.31 in 2025 grew 7% YoY, with 2026 guidance of $6.55-$6.80 and a reaffirmed 5-7% long-term EPS growth target. The dividend profile offers predictability — 43 consecutive years paid, 20 consecutive years of growth, 3.58% current yield, and a $103B five-year capital plan that supports continued regulated earnings growth [3][4]. Forward P/E of 16.9 is attractive for a utility with improving growth visibility from data center demand.
thesis_continued: The bear case for Duke Energy centers on the tension between its capital-intensive growth plan and its financial constraints. D/E of 162% reflects the massive capital requirements of a regulated utility executing a $103B investment plan, and the company's free cash flow is deeply negative (-$4.5B TTM) as capital spending far exceeds operating cash flow [4]. The 2.0% five-year dividend growth CAGR significantly trails inflation, meaning real income is declining for dividend investors — the 3.58% yield must compensate for minimal growth. ROE of 9.9% is constrained by the regulated return model, and revenue growth of 1.1% in the most recent quarter highlights the slow organic growth reality between rate cases. Regulatory execution risk is significant — the data center agreements and capital plan depend on state utility commissions approving rate increases, and any pushback could compress returns on the massive investment. The CEO transition from Lynn Good to Harry Sideris introduces incremental execution risk during the most capital-intensive period in the company's history [1][3].
key_catalysts: AI data center electricity demand — 7.8 GW of service agreements secured with 15.4 GW in late-stage pipeline expected to convert by H1 2027, potentially adding $5-10B to the five-year capital plan with minimum-take provisions that support revenue visibility [1][2]

Regulated earnings growth trajectory — 2026 adjusted EPS guidance of $6.55-$6.80 (up 4-8% YoY) with management reaffirming 5-7% long-term growth targets, expected to hit the upper half of the range starting 2028 as data center demand accelerates [1][2]

Clean energy transition investments — $103B five-year capital plan supporting grid modernization, renewable generation, and nuclear expansion creates a decades-long regulated asset growth runway with rate-base recovery [3]
key_risks: Regulatory execution risk — the $103B capital plan and data center interconnection strategy depend on state utility commissions approving rate increases to support massive infrastructure investment, and any regulatory pushback could compress returns on invested capital [1][3]

Dividend growth stagnation — the 2.0% five-year dividend growth CAGR trails inflation, and with a 64.2% payout ratio, limited free cash flow, and D/E of 162%, the company faces constraints on accelerating dividend growth while funding its capital plan [4]

Capital structure strain — deeply negative free cash flow of -$4.5B TTM with $92.2B in total debt reflects the massive capital requirements of the investment plan, and rising interest rates could increase funding costs for the sustained debt issuance required to finance the $103B program [3][4]
